strengths: The method is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: predicting normalized temporal distances between frame pairs and using adjacent-frame distances as step-wise rewards is an elegant formulation with implicit negative sampling (antisymmetry), exponentially weighted pair sampling for fine-grained resolution, and two-hot discretization.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 10 Meta-World tasks, 8 baselines across three methodological categories, 8 seeds per run with mean ± s.d. reporting, ablations of every design component, and alternative temporal modeling designs (only-from-init, single-frame, order prediction) in the appendix.

Fairness efforts are commendable: VIP is retrained with both ResNet34 and ViT backbones, all RL baselines use the same DrQ-v2 backbone, and the demonstration collection protocol (diverse initializations) is honestly documented as deliberately harder for occupation-matching baselines.

The qualitative analysis (Figure 4) directly probes the central claimed property — distinguishing successful from failed rollouts under distribution shift — and the VOC evaluation on held-out videos tests generalization beyond memorization.

The cross-domain experiment with real human videos (single/multi-view) combined with only 1 in-domain demonstration is a compelling demonstration of scalability beyond simulation-only demonstrations, and the limitations (back-and-forth tasks) are honestly acknowledged.
Surpassing the manually designed dense environment reward on 9/10 tasks, if accurate, is a practically significant result for reducing reward engineering effort.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification (Section 4.3) is thin: Equations 8–9 essentially assume expert optimality and per-step uniform cost and then derive that temporal distance aligns with progress, which is close to circular; there is no theorem, no proof, and no discussion of what happens when experts are suboptimal or demonstrations have variable lengths.

Conceptual novelty is modest: progress/temporal-structure-based rewards are well explored (TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, GVL), and TimeRewarder is best viewed as a careful recombination and simplification (direct distance regression vs. ranking/triples) rather than a fundamentally new idea; the paper would benefit from a crisper statement of what is genuinely new versus inherited.

All quantitative RL results are confined to Meta-World; the real-world component only supplies human videos as reward-model training data while policy learning remains in simulation, so claims about real-world applicability are only partially supported.

The claim that out-of-distribution generalization is superior relies on qualitative trajectory visualizations (Figure 4) and VOC on held-out expert videos rather than a systematic quantitative study on distribution-shifted agent rollouts.
The project page is empty ('Project page:') and no code release is stated, which weakens reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

Some design choices (e.g., K=20 bins, λ for exponential sampling, α weight for the sparse success signal) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, and the dependence on the sparse success signal is not fully disentangled in the main results (only in Appendix A.3.2, where proxy-only performance is substantially weaker).

strengths: The method is clearly presented and simple: a progress model Fθ trained to predict normalized temporal distances between frame pairs, with implicit negative sampling, exponentially weighted pair sampling, and two-hot discretization, then frozen during RL.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: ten Meta-World tasks, eight baselines across three categories (including privileged references like BC and environment dense reward), eight seeds per run, an out-of-distribution generalization test via the VOC metric (Figure 3), qualitative reward-shaping analysis (Figure 4), a full component-wise ablation study (Figure 7), an experiment without the sparse success signal (A.3.2), a backbone-controlled comparison against VIP (A.3.1), and cross-domain human-video experiments (Figure 6).

The observation that a frozen reward model trained only on expert data avoids the online-refinement instability reported by Rank2Reward and PROGRESSOR is a practically meaningful property, and the qualitative Figure 4 analysis supports the claim of better OOD reward behavior.

The diverse-initialization demonstration protocol (A.4.2) is a thoughtful attempt to prevent pixel-level shortcut alignment between agent and expert data, and the appendix honestly explains why it disadvantages OT/ADS-style baselines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea — exploiting temporal ordering/structure of demonstration videos as task progress — is well established (TCN, VIP, GVL, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR). The contribution is essentially a regression variant of these ranking/ordering objectives with engineering refinements (weighted sampling, two-hot discretization borrowed from Wang et al., 2024). The framing as a conceptual advance is overstated relative to what is incremental work.

The 'theoretical justification' in Section 4.3 is near-trivial. Equations 8-9 assume expert optimality and define the potential so that the Bellman equation holds by construction; it does not provide any guarantee about rewards on out-of-distribution agent states, which is the actual difficulty of the problem. Calling this a justification that 'temporal distance aligns naturally with task progress' overstates its content.

The headline claim that TimeRewarder 'outperforms the manually designed environment dense reward' is weakened by the setup: the final reward (Eq. 7) combines the proxy reward with the sparse binary success signal, and A.3.2 shows that with proxy reward only, no task reaches success within the budget. The comparison to environment reward is therefore not apples-to-apples (shaped reward + sparse bonus vs. dense reward alone), and the claim of surpassing the 'upper bound' deserves much more careful qualification than it receives.

The demonstration protocol change in A.4.2 that broadens initial-state distributions deliberately degrades OT/ADS baselines. While the real-world motivation is defensible, it means the strongest comparison against prior imitation-from-observation methods is conducted under conditions chosen partly to disadvantage them, and no results under the standard narrow-initialization protocol are reported as a control.

Evaluation is confined to simulation (Meta-World). The cross-domain 'real-world' experiments in Question 4 use human videos for reward learning but still train the policy in Meta-World simulation with as few as one in-domain demonstration; there is no real-robot RL evaluation, which limits the significance of the scalability claims for robotics.

The project page entry on page 1 is empty and no code release is mentioned. For a paper whose central contribution is an empirical comparison across many reimplemented baselines (retrained VIP, modified PROGRESSOR/Rank2Reward integrations, custom demonstration protocol), reproducibility is a serious concern.

Limitations are discussed only in one sentence in the conclusion (failure on tasks with frequent back-and-forth motions); given that the method assumes monotone, single-modal expert trajectories, a more substantive treatment of when the frame-wise temporal-distance assumption breaks (multi-stage tasks, loops, time-varying speed) is needed.

Several baselines are run under potentially non-ideal configurations despite appendix mitigations (e.g., VIP's optimization instability is asserted rather than evidenced with tuning details), which leaves open whether the margins over progress-based baselines are methodological or tuning artifacts.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-structured empirical evaluation: 10 Meta-World tasks with 8 seeds, 8 baselines spanning three methodological categories (progress-based reward learning, ILfO, privileged references), plus dedicated evaluation of reward quality (VOC metric on held-out expert videos, Figure 3) and reward behavior under distribution shift (Figure 4), which goes beyond the usual 'just show final RL curves' evaluation.

The method addresses a known failure mode of prior progress-based reward methods (Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR overestimating progress on out-of-distribution states) through implicit negative sampling, and the ablations (Figure 7) cleanly isolate the contribution of each component (negatives, weighted sampling, discretization) with task-specific explanations for why each matters.

Cross-domain experiments (Figure 6) demonstrating that real-world human videos can be combined with a single in-domain demonstration to improve RL is a valuable step toward the scalability argument, and the appendix transparently documents the human video datasets and collection protocol.

Additional controls in the appendix strengthen the claims: VIP re-trained with the same ViT backbone (A.3.1), RL with only proxy reward and no sparse success signal (A.3.2), alternative temporal modeling designs (A.4.1), and full hyperparameter tables supporting reproducibility.
The paper is clearly written with a logical four-question structure for the experiments, and limitations (failure on back-and-forth motions) are honestly acknowledged in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Section 4.3 is shallow: Equation (8) essentially defines a potential from a uniform step cost on expert trajectories, and the Bellman-style relation (Equation 9) follows almost by construction under expert optimality. It formalizes a definition rather than proving a nontrivial property of the learned model or generalization behavior, so it does not substantively support the central empirical claims.

Originality is incremental. The core idea—predicting relative temporal position/order between frames as a progress signal—is closely related to Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, VIP, and GVL, and the components (two-hot discretization borrowed from Wang et al., 2024; exponentially weighted sampling; symmetric/antisymmetric targets) are fairly natural combinations. The contribution rests mainly on empirical refinement rather than a new concept.

Evidence is confined to a single simulation benchmark (Meta-World) with only 10 manipulation tasks, plus 3 tasks in the human-video setting. All results are script-policy-generated demonstrations on relatively short-horizon tasks; generalization to longer-horizon or more dexterous settings remains untested, limiting the significance of the scalability claim.

The comparison protocol could favor the proposed method: the deliberately broadened initialization range (Appendix A.4.2) is justified as more realistic, but it knowingly degrades occupancy-matching baselines (OT, ADS). Baseline-tuning choices like goal-frame provisioning for VIP/PROGRESSOR are reasonable, yet the overall fairness depends on details the authors control.

The headline claim of surpassing the manually designed dense environment reward (9/10 tasks) is striking but should be interpreted cautiously: the environment-reward baseline uses only dense reward, while TimeRewarder additionally receives the sparse binary success signal (Equation 7), a non-identical comparison; and one task is not solved, suggesting some sensitivity.

No code release or project page content is provided ('Project page:' is empty), which weakens reproducibility despite the thorough hyperparameter documentation; and the cross-domain result depends on carefully matched real-world task replicas collected by the authors, which other groups cannot easily reproduce.

strengths: The core idea—learning frame-wise, signed temporal distances from action-free videos and using them as step-wise dense rewards—is simple, well-motivated, and cleanly instantiated; the antisymmetric signed-distance formulation naturally provides suboptimality awareness without extra objectives.

Comprehensive and fair evaluation: 10 Meta-World tasks with 8 seeds per experiment, unified CLIP ViT-B backbone for progress-based baselines, unified DrQ-v2 for all RL baselines, VOC-based reward quality analysis, qualitative rollout analyses (Fig. 4, 5), and extensive ablations of every design component (implicit negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, discretization, alternative temporal modeling variants).

Strong empirical results: nearly perfect success on 9/10 tasks with 200k interactions, outperforming all baselines and even hand-crafted dense environment rewards on most tasks, with additional appendix comparisons to OT-based methods (TemporalIOT, ORCA), BC, BCO, a from-scratch backbone ablation, and a second simulator (ManiSkill3).

Cross-domain experiments with real human videos (single- and multi-view) demonstrate practical scalability beyond simulation, and the combination of 1 in-domain demo + 20 human videos substantially improves over human-video-only training.

The appendix proof of VIP's unbounded loss (A.3) is a useful diagnostic contribution, and the paper is honest about limitations (visual aliasing under back-and-forth motions, history-augmentation workaround, sensitivity discussion in the conclusion).
Well written with a clear question-driven experimental structure and detailed hyperparameter tables supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the idea of temporal/progress-based reward shaping from demonstrations builds directly on TCC, TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, and PROGRESSOR; the contribution is primarily a better-formulated objective (regression of signed temporal distances with discretization and sampling biases) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical justification (Sec. 4.3) is limited to a deterministic, fully observable chain MDP with the optimal policy; the connection to visual POMDPs is acknowledged informally but not formally treated, so the theory mainly motivates rather than guarantees the method.

Downstream RL still uses a sparse success signal combined with the learned dense reward (Eq. 7); while proxy-reward-only results appear in the appendix and perform worse, the headline claims partly depend on this privileged binary success signal.

The method assumes expert videos with monotonic task progress and task-relevant visual discriminability; failure cases with frequent back-and-forth motions are acknowledged but only heuristically addressed via history stacking, and no real-world robotics deployment is shown (cross-domain evaluation is reward learning + simulated RL).
Task selection is limited to Meta-World manipulation (plus one ManiSkill task), all with scripted expert videos; generality to more diverse or long-horizon in-the-wild videos remains untested.

strengths: The method is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: signed frame-wise temporal distance prediction with implicit negative sampling (reversed frame pairs), weighted pair sampling for fine-grained resolution, and two-hot discretization are each intuitively justified and individually ablated (Figure 8, Appendix A.5.1).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 10 Meta-World tasks with 8 seeds, eight baselines across three method families plus privileged references, VOC-based reward quality analysis (Figure 3), qualitative reward-shape analysis on success vs. failure rollouts (Figure 4), representation visualizations (Figure 5), additional OT-based baselines (A.4.4), a second simulator (ManiSkill3, A.4.9), hyperparameter sensitivity for α and K, and a from-scratch backbone ablation (A.4.3).

The cross-domain experiment with real human videos (single-view and multi-view, Figure 7) is a meaningful step beyond purely synthetic evaluation, and the finding that human-only data underperforms but helps when combined with a single in-domain demo is honest and useful.

The appendix contains a substantive analysis of the VIP objective's unboundedness (A.3) and a fair-play ablation adding negative sampling to PROGRESSOR (A.4.8), which strengthens the argument that the gains come from the representation structure rather than trivial optimization differences.
Limitations (visual aliasing under back-and-forth motions) are acknowledged rather than hidden, with a proposed (though not fully evaluated) history-based mitigation.
weaknesses: The headline claim that TimeRewarder 'outperforms the manually designed environment dense reward' deserves more scrutiny: the final reward (Eq. 7) combines the learned proxy reward with the sparse environment success signal, and the exact composition of the environment-dense-reward baseline (whether it also receives the sparse signal) is not fully specified. A significant portion of the claimed superiority may come from the added sparse term rather than the learned dense component.

The theoretical justification (Section 4.3) relies on strong assumptions: fully observable state, deterministic transitions, and optimality of the demonstration policy. It essentially shows that temporal distance is a valid potential function in an idealized chain MDP; the gap between this analysis and the POMDP/visual-aliasing setting the authors themselves flag (e.g., the o1 revisiting example) is bridged only verbally, and the proposed history-window fix is not experimentally evaluated.

Novelty is modest: the core idea is a regression head on CLIP frame pairs predicting normalized temporal position, with components borrowed from prior work (two-hot discretization from WDreamer-style approaches, progress-from-video concepts from TCC/TCN/Rank2Reward/PROGRESSOR). The paper's case rests mainly on the specific combination and engineering rather than a fundamentally new insight.

The demonstration collection protocol deliberately broadens initialization states (A.5.2). While well-argued as more realistic, this change demonstrably disadvantages OT-based baselines (OT, ADS, TemporalIOT), and the paper does not report results under the standard narrow-initialization protocol, so it is hard to fully rule out that the benchmark setup flatters the proposed method.

Real-world evaluation is limited to reward learning from human videos; all policy learning is in simulation, and the human-video experiments cover only 3 of 10 tasks. The 'scalable watch-to-act' narrative is thus more aspirational than demonstrated.

Some evidence is presented in a way that is hard to verify: e.g., Question 2 analyses use only two hand-picked trajectories per task, and several key comparisons (e.g., environment dense reward vs. proxy-only, A.4.5) appear only in the appendix where the proxy-only results show the method alone does not solve most tasks within budget.

strengths: The method is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: learning signed frame-wise temporal distances from action-free videos, with three well-justified design choices (implicit negative sampling via frame order, weighted pair sampling for fine-grained resolution, two-hot discretization for stability).

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: 10 Meta-World tasks, 8+ baselines spanning three method families, 8 seeds per run, held-out demonstration generalization tests (VOC metric), qualitative reward analyses on successful vs. failed rollouts, representation-space analysis, and extensive ablations of every proposed component.

The headline result is compelling: TimeRewarder outperforms both learned reward baselines and the manually engineered dense environment reward on 9/10 tasks with only 200k interactions, and the paper honestly notes and ablates the dependence on the sparse success signal (Appendix A.4.5).

The cross-domain experiments with real human videos (single-view and multi-view, 20 videos per task, with only 1 in-domain demo) are a meaningful step beyond simulation-only evaluation and directly support the claimed scalability.

The appendix adds substantial value: a proof that the VIP objective (as implemented in its codebase) is unbounded and admits degenerate solutions, additional OT-based baselines, a PROGRESSOR augmentation ablation showing the gap is structural rather than data-driven, hyperparameter tables, sensitivity analyses for alpha and discretization bins, and a second simulator (ManiSkill3).
Limitations are discussed candidly: the single-frame POMDP visual-aliasing issue in back-and-forth motions, with a concrete proposed mitigation (history-window inputs).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification (Section 4.3) rests on strong assumptions — fully observable MDP, deterministic transitions, and a visual encoder that uniquely identifies each task phase — which the authors themselves acknowledge are violated in visual RL; the theory is therefore more of a motivating argument than a guarantee, and the connection to the learned objective is informal.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior progress-based reward learning (TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, GVL); the contribution is primarily a cleaner formulation plus careful engineering rather than a fundamentally new idea, though the empirical evidence justifies it.

Demonstrations come from Meta-World's scripted (near-optimal) policies with a deliberately broadened initialization; the claim of robustness to in-the-wild videos is only partially tested (3 tasks, 20 curated human videos per task, fixed task setups).

Main RL results combine the proxy reward with the environment's sparse success signal (Eq. 7), so the 'learned from videos' claim is strongest only in the appendix ablation; per-task adaptive alpha, while shown insensitive in Figure 12, adds a mild fairness concern for baseline comparisons.

The demonstration diversity protocol in A.5.2 is non-standard for Meta-World, making direct comparison with prior published results on this benchmark difficult (though the authors justify this and provide the needed baselines under the same protocol).
